nodes.label: Resources of collecting data
nodes.description: Distinguish primary (field) resources — interviews and questionnaires, accurate but costly in time/effort/money — from secondary (historical) resources — agencies (e.g. CAPMAS), internet, media — which save time and money.

nodes.label: Methods of collecting data: mass population vs samples
nodes.description: Compare the method of mass population (census: all the society, unbiased, very accurate, but long time/effort/cost) with methods of samples (save time/effort/money; the only way for gigantic societies and for destructive tests); recognize biased samples.

nodes.label: Biased vs random selection; simple random sample
nodes.description: Distinguish biased (deliberate) selection from random selection where every member has an equal chance; apply the simple random sample to a homogeneous society (cards in a box for small societies; calculator random digits for big societies).

nodes.label: Layer (stratified) random sample
nodes.description: For a heterogeneous society, divide it into homogeneous layers and select from each layer a random sample proportional to the layer's size in the society.

nodes.label: Dispersion and the range
nodes.description: Explain dispersion (how divergent the values of a set are; zero dispersion means all values equal); compute the range = greatest value − smallest value; know its limits: influenced greatly by outliers and depends only on the two extreme values.

nodes.label: Standard deviation of a set of values
nodes.description: Compute σ = √(Σ(x−x̄)²/n): find the mean, the deviations from the mean, their squares, the average of the squares, then the positive square root.

nodes.label: Standard deviation of a frequency distribution
nodes.description: Compute σ = √(Σ(x−x̄)²k / Σk) with x̄ = Σxk/Σk for a frequency distribution; for grouped data (sets/classes) use the center of each set as x.

nodes.label: Comparing dispersion and homogeneity of data sets
nodes.description: Use range and standard deviation to compare sets with the same measuring units and equal means: the set with the smaller standard deviation is more homogeneous (less dispersed); σ is affected by all values and carries the units of the data.

questions.stem: A researcher collects data by distributing a questionnaire (survey) to families and interviewing them. This is a … resource of collecting data.
solution: Primary (field) resources are those from which we originally get the data ourselves, through interviewing or questionnaires (surveys).
A questionnaire distributed to families is exactly this case, so it is a primary (field) resource.
Secondary (historical) resources would be ready-made data from agencies, the internet or media.
questions.source_note: Original question; scope of Lesson 3-1, resources of collecting data, p.38

questions.stem: A student takes ready-made data about Egypt's population from the records of the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics. This data comes from a … resource.
solution: Secondary (historical) resources are data we get from authorities and agencies that formally work in statistics, such as the central agency for mobilization and statistics, the internet and the media.
The student did not collect the data himself; he used the agency's ready records, so it is a secondary (historical) resource.
questions.source_note: Original question; secondary resources definition, p.38

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of secondary (historical) resources of collecting data?

choices.text: They are the most accurate of all resources
They require interviewing every member of the society
They need great time and effort

solution: Secondary (historical) resources give us data that is already collected by agencies, the internet or the media.
Because the data is ready-made, this type of resource saves time and money.
Accuracy is the distinguishing advantage of primary (field) resources, and needing great time and effort is a disadvantage of primary resources — not of secondary ones.
questions.source_note: Original question; advantages of secondary resources, p.38

questions.stem: Primary (field) resources of collecting data are distinguished by … but they …

choices.text: accuracy; need much time, effort and money
speed; cannot be used for surveys
saving money; depend on the media

solution: Primary (field) resources — interviewing and questionnaires — are distinguished by accuracy, because we collect the data originally ourselves.
However, they need time and effort, and conducting them is highly expensive.
So the correct completion is: distinguished by accuracy, but need much time, effort and money.
questions.source_note: Original question; advantages/disadvantages of primary resources, p.38

questions.stem: Four students collected data for a statistics project. Which student used a PRIMARY (field) resource?

choices.text: Hany, who copied population figures from a newspaper report
Mona, who interviewed shoppers about a new product at the market
Omar, who downloaded last year's exam statistics from the ministry website
Sara, who used tables published by a statistics agency

solution: Primary (field) resources are those where we originally get the data ourselves through interviewing or questionnaires.
Only Mona collected data directly from the people concerned (interviewing shoppers), so she used a primary resource.
Newspapers, websites and agency tables are ready-made data — these are secondary (historical) resources.
questions.source_note: Original scenario question; classifying resources of collecting data, p.38

questions.stem: The method of collecting data that includes ALL the values of the statistical society is called the method of …
solution: The method of mass population means to collect the data related to the phenomenon from all the society (like a full population census).
It includes all the values, so it is unbiased and its outcomes are very accurate — but it needs long time, great effort and much money.
questions.source_note: Original question; method of mass population definition, pp.38-39

questions.stem: To collect data about the fish of the Mediterranean Sea, we must use the method of …, because the society is gigantic.
solution: One advantage of the methods of samples is that they are the only way to collect data about gigantic societies, like fish.
We cannot count or examine every fish in the sea, so we study a sample and generalize the outcomes on the whole society.
questions.source_note: Original question; advantages of sample methods (gigantic societies), p.39

questions.stem: A factory checks the validity of the electric lamps it produces (how long a lamp can be used before getting burned) using a sample only. Why?

choices.text: Because samples always give more accurate outcomes than a census
Because the test consumes the lamp, so testing all the production would destroy it
Because the number of lamps is too small for a census
Because lamps form a heterogeneous society

solution: The sample method is the only method to study some limited societies where the examination destroys the unit under test.
Knowing how long a lamp can be used means running it until it gets burned — so a tested lamp cannot be sold.
Testing all the production would destroy it; therefore the factory tests a sample only (like checking a patient's blood by a small sample).
questions.source_note: Original question; sample as the only method for destructive tests, p.39

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of the method of mass population?

choices.text: It saves time, effort and money
It is the only way to study gigantic societies
It includes all the values, so it is unbiased and its outcomes are very accurate
It needs a very small number of researchers

solution: The method of mass population collects the data from all the society.
Because it includes all the values, it is unbiased and its outcomes are very accurate.
Saving time, effort and money — and studying gigantic societies — are advantages of the methods of samples, not of the mass population method.
questions.source_note: Original question; advantages of mass population vs samples, pp.38-39

questions.stem: A researcher selected a sample, but it does not represent all the society well, so the outcomes are not accurate. Such a sample is called …
solution: A disadvantage of the sample methods is that the outcomes are not accurate if the selected sample does not represent all the society well.
In such a case the sample is called biased.
questions.source_note: Original question; biased sample definition, p.39

questions.stem: In random selection (random samples), the sample is selected such that …

choices.text: it satisfies the objectives of the research deliberately
the chance of getting any value from the society is equal
only the best members of the society are chosen

solution: Random selection means to select a sample such that the chance of getting any value from the society is equal.
Selecting the sample deliberately to satisfy the research objectives is the biased selection, and including the whole society is the mass population method.
questions.source_note: Original question; random selection definition, p.39

questions.stem: The simple random sample is the simplest type of samples, and it is taken from the … societies.
solution: The simple random sample is the simplest type of samples.
It is taken from the homogeneous societies, where selection is related only to the size and number of units in the society.
When the society is heterogeneous (made of different sets), we use the layer sample instead.
questions.source_note: Original question; simple random sample definition, p.39

questions.stem: To choose 4 students from a class of 36, the teacher writes each student's name on an identical card, puts all the cards in a box, draws one card randomly, records it, returns it, and repeats until 4 different students are obtained. This sample is …
solution: All the cards are identical and are drawn randomly from the box, so every student has an equal chance of being selected.
This is exactly the simple random sample procedure for a small society: prepare identical cards, draw randomly, return the card, and repeat until the needed sample is obtained.
The class is one homogeneous group (no layers), so it is a simple random sample.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the 5-of-40 cards example, p.39 (new numbers)

questions.stem: To know how the students understood a mathematics lesson, a teacher analyzed the test outcomes of ONLY the group of students who had studied that same topic together before. This selection is …
solution: The teacher selected the sample deliberately, in a way that satisfies the objectives of the research: only students who studied the same topic.
The other students had no chance of being selected, so the chances are not equal.
This is the biased selection (samples not randomly selected).
questions.source_note: Original question; biased selection example (teacher scenario), p.39

questions.stem: The students of a school are numbered from 1 to 600. To select a simple random sample, a calculator gave the random numbers $0.624,\ 0.871,\ 0.315,\ 0.598,\ 0.042$. After taking out the decimal point (making numbers from 0 to 999), how many of these five numbers can be used for the sample?
solution: Taking out the decimal point turns each number into a whole number from 0 to 999: $624,\ 871,\ 315,\ 598,\ 042 = 42$.
Only numbers within the field of the students' numbers (1 to 600) can be used; numbers more than 600 are taken out.
$624 > 600$ (rejected), $871 > 600$ (rejected), $315 \le 600$ (accepted), $598 \le 600$ (accepted), $42 \le 600$ (accepted).
So $3$ of the five numbers can be used.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the calculator random-digits method (society of 800 → 600, new digits), p.40

questions.stem: When the society to be examined is heterogeneous (made up of sets different in characteristics), we divide it into homogeneous sets and select from each one. The suitable sample is the … sample.
solution: When the society is heterogeneous, it is divided into homogeneous sets according to the characteristics forming it; each set is called a layer.
The researcher selects a random sample in which each layer is represented according to its size in the society — such a sample is called the layer sample.
questions.source_note: Original question; layer random sample definition, p.40

questions.stem: A society consists of 600 persons where the ratio of males to females is $2 : 1$. To select a layer sample of 60 persons, how many males must be selected?
solution: The ratio of males to females is $2 : 1$, so the society consists of $2 + 1 = 3$ equal parts.
Each layer must be represented in the sample according to its size: the males' share is $\frac{2}{3}$ of the sample.
Number of males $= \frac{2}{3} \times 60 = 40$ persons (and the females are $\frac{1}{3} \times 60 = 20$).
questions.source_note: Original variant of the layer-sample example (400 persons, 3:2, sample 50 → new numbers), p.40

questions.stem: A school has 900 students distributed over the three preparatory grades in the ratio $4 : 3 : 2$ (first : second : third). In a layer sample of 90 students, how many students of the THIRD grade must be selected?
solution: The society is heterogeneous (three different grades), so each grade is a layer represented according to its size.
The ratio parts total $4 + 3 + 2 = 9$ parts; the third grade's share is $\frac{2}{9}$.
Number of third-grade students in the sample $= \frac{2}{9} \times 90 = 20$ students.
questions.source_note: Original question; layer sample with a three-layer ratio, extends p.40 example

questions.stem: A society of 1500 persons contains a layer of 600 persons. In a layer sample of 75 persons taken from the whole society, how many persons must come from that layer?
solution: In the layer sample, each layer is represented in the sample according to its size in the society.
The layer's share of the society $= \frac{600}{1500} = \frac{2}{5}$.
Number selected from that layer $= \frac{2}{5} \times 75 = 30$ persons.
questions.source_note: Original question; proportional layer allocation from layer size, p.40

questions.stem: In the layer random sample, each layer is represented in the sample according to …

choices.text: the alphabetical order of its members
an equal share for every layer regardless of size

solution: After dividing the heterogeneous society into homogeneous layers, the researcher selects a random sample from each layer.
Each layer is represented according to its size in the society — for example, a society of 400 with males : females $= 3 : 2$ and a sample of 50 gives 30 males and 20 females.
Equal shares regardless of size would not represent the society well (a biased sample).
questions.source_note: Original question; proportional representation rule of the layer sample, p.40

questions.stem: Find the range of the values: $7,\ 12,\ 9,\ 15,\ 10$.
solution: The range is the difference between the greatest value and the smallest value in the set.
The greatest value $= 15$ and the smallest value $= 7$.
questions.source_note: Original question; range definition (cf. first/second set example, p.42)

questions.stem: If the dispersion of a set of values equals zero, then …
solution: Dispersion measures how divergent the values are — the differences between the values.
When the dispersion is zero, there are no differences between the values: all the values are equal.
questions.source_note: Original question; dispersion definition box, p.42

questions.stem: The range of a set of values is 25 and its smallest value is 13. Find the greatest value.
solution: Range $=$ greatest value $-$ smallest value.
So greatest value $=$ range $+$ smallest value $= 25 + 13 = 38$.
questions.source_note: Original question; reverse use of the range rule, p.42

questions.stem: The range does not give a clear picture of the dispersion of a set because it depends only on …

choices.text: the greatest and the smallest values
the middle value of the set

solution: The range is influenced only by the two extreme values: range $=$ greatest $-$ smallest.
It is not influenced by any value in the set except the greatest and smallest values, so it does not give a clear picture of the dispersion of the whole set.
It is also influenced greatly by the outlier.
questions.source_note: Original question; notices (2) and (3) on the range, pp.42-43

questions.stem: For the set $41,\ 44,\ 46,\ 48,\ 90$: find how much the range DECREASES when the outlier 90 is removed from the set.
solution: Range of the whole set $= 90 - 41 = 49$.
After removing the outlier 90, the greatest value becomes 48, so the range $= 48 - 41 = 7$.
The decrease in the range $= 49 - 7 = 42$ — this shows that the range is influenced greatly by the outlier.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the outlier notice (second set 42..92, remove 92), p.42

questions.stem: The standard deviation $\sigma$ of a set of values is the positive square root of …

choices.text: the sum of the values divided by their range
the difference between the greatest and smallest values
the average of the squares of deviations of the values from the mean

solution: By definition, the standard deviation is the positive square root of the average of the squares of deviations of the values from the mean.
In symbols: $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n}}$, where $\bar{x}$ is the mean and $n$ is the number of values.
questions.source_note: Original question; standard deviation definition and formula, p.43

questions.stem: Find the standard deviation of the values: $6,\ 6,\ 6,\ 6$.
solution: The mean $\bar{x} = \dfrac{6+6+6+6}{4} = \dfrac{24}{4} = 6$.
Every deviation $x - \bar{x} = 6 - 6 = 0$, so $\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 = 0$.
$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{0}{4}} = 0$ — when all the values are equal, the dispersion is zero.
questions.source_note: Original question; σ of equal values links to zero dispersion, pp.42-43

questions.stem: Calculate the standard deviation of the values: $7,\ 9,\ 10,\ 11,\ 13$.
solution: Find the mean: $\bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum x}{n} = \dfrac{7+9+10+11+13}{5} = \dfrac{50}{5} = 10$.
Form the table of deviations $x - \bar{x}$: $-3,\ -1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 3$.
Square the deviations $(x - \bar{x})^2$: $9,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 9$, so $\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 = 20$.
$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{20}{5}} = \sqrt{4} = 2$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the worked example (values 12,13,16,18,21 → new values, same table method), p.43

questions.stem: The standard deviation of the values $3,\ 5,\ 5,\ 7$ equals …
solution: The mean $\bar{x} = \dfrac{3+5+5+7}{4} = \dfrac{20}{4} = 5$.
Deviations from the mean: $-2,\ 0,\ 0,\ 2$; their squares: $4,\ 0,\ 0,\ 4$, so $\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 = 8$.
$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{8}{4}} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$.
questions.source_note: Original question; σ table method with n = 4, p.43

questions.stem: For a set of 5 values, the sum of the squares of deviations from the mean is $\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 = 45$. Find the standard deviation.
solution: $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n}}$ where $n$ is the number of values.
Substitute: $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{45}{5}} = \sqrt{9}$.
$\sigma = 3$.
questions.source_note: Original question; applying the σ formula directly, p.43

questions.stem: When calculating the standard deviation of a frequency distribution of SETS (classes), $x$ in the formula $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x-\bar{x})^2\, k}{\sum k}}$ represents …
solution: In the frequency-distribution formula, $x$ represents the value or the center of the set, and $k$ represents the frequency of the value or the set.
For a distribution of sets (classes), we first find the center of each set and use it as $x$; $\sum k$ is the total of frequencies.
questions.source_note: Original question; symbols of the frequency-distribution σ formula, pp.44-45

questions.stem: In the frequency distribution with sets $0-,\ 4-,\ 8-,\ 12-,\ 16\text{-}20$, find the center of the set $12-$.
solution: The center of a set is half the sum of its two boundaries: the set $12-$ extends from 12 to 16.
questions.source_note: Original question; centers of sets step from the marks example, p.45

questions.stem: The following frequency distribution shows the goals scored in 10 football matches — goals: $0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4$; number of matches: $1,\ 1,\ 6,\ 1,\ 1$. Find the standard deviation of the number of goals.
solution: Total of frequencies $\sum k = 1+1+6+1+1 = 10$.
$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x-\bar{x})^2 k}{\sum k}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{10}{10}} = \sqrt{1} = 1$ goal.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the goals drill (7 matches table → new frequencies), p.45

questions.stem: The marks of 16 students are grouped in the sets $0-,\ 10-,\ 20\text{-}30$ with frequencies $2,\ 12,\ 2$. Find the standard deviation of the marks.
solution: Find the centers of the sets: $\dfrac{0+10}{2}=5$, $\dfrac{10+20}{2}=15$, $\dfrac{20+30}{2}=25$ — use them as $x$.
$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x-\bar{x})^2 k}{\sum k}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{400}{16}} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ marks.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the 40-students grouped-marks example (new classes and frequencies, same 6-step method), pp.45-46

questions.stem: The numbers of defective units found in 50 boxes: defective units $0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4$ with numbers of boxes $5,\ 10,\ 20,\ 10,\ 5$. The standard deviation of the defective units equals …
solution: The mean $\bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum xk}{\sum k} = \dfrac{100}{50} = 2$ units.
$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{60}{50}} = \sqrt{1.2} \approx 1.095$ units — note $1.2$ alone (choice B) forgets the square root, and $2$ (choice A) is the mean, not $\sigma$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the defective-units example (100 boxes → 50 boxes, new frequencies), p.44

questions.stem: Two sets of data have the same measuring units and equal means. The MORE HOMOGENEOUS set is the one whose …
solution: The standard deviation is used to compare the dispersion of sets which have the same measuring units when the means are equal.
The set which has the greater standard deviation is more dispersed; so the more homogeneous set is the one with the smaller standard deviation.
questions.source_note: Original question; notice (2) on comparing dispersion, p.47

questions.stem: In an exam, class A has mean 25 marks with $\sigma = 3.2$ marks, and class B has mean 25 marks with $\sigma = 5.6$ marks. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Class B is more homogeneous in getting marks
Class A is more homogeneous in getting marks
The two classes have the same dispersion
We cannot compare them because the means are equal

solution: The two distributions have the same units (marks) and equal means (25), so we compare their standard deviations.
$\sigma_A = 3.2 < \sigma_B = 5.6$, so class B's marks are more dispersed.
Therefore class A is more homogeneous in getting marks — equal means is exactly the condition that MAKES the comparison valid.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the two-classes drill (compare σ of classes A and B), p.47

questions.stem: Set A: $10,\ 12,\ 14$ and Set B: $5,\ 12,\ 19$. How many times is the range of set B as great as the range of set A?
solution: Range of set A $= 14 - 10 = 4$.
Range of set B $= 19 - 5 = 14$.
$\dfrac{\text{range of B}}{\text{range of A}} = \dfrac{14}{4} = 3.5$ times — set B is more divergent (more dispersed) than set A.
questions.source_note: Original question; comparing dispersion of two sets by the range, p.42

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the standard deviation is CORRECT?

choices.text: It depends only on the greatest and smallest values
It is not affected by the outlier
It is affected by the deviations of all the values, and it has the same measuring units as the original data

solution: Notice (1): the standard deviation is affected by the deviations of ALL the values, and its value is affected by the outlier — unlike the range, which depends only on the two extremes.
Notice (2): the standard deviation has the same measuring units as the original data (e.g. marks, units, pounds).
So D is the correct statement.
questions.source_note: Original question; notices (1) and (2) on σ, p.47

questions.stem: Set A: $8,\ 9,\ 10,\ 11,\ 12$ and Set B: $6,\ 8,\ 10,\ 12,\ 14$ (both have mean 10). How many times is the standard deviation of set B as great as the standard deviation of set A?
solution: Both sets have mean $\bar{x} = \dfrac{50}{5} = 10$, so we compare dispersion by the standard deviation.
$\dfrac{\sigma_B}{\sigma_A} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = 2$ — set B is twice as dispersed, so set A is more homogeneous.
questions.source_note: Original question; comparing σ of two sets with equal means, p.47

visuals.caption: Answers from our own ice-cream survey — data we collect ourselves is a primary (field) resource.
Ready-made data from agencies, the internet and the media — secondary (historical) resources save time and money.
A census asks all 800 students; a sample asks only 40 and generalizes the outcomes on the whole society.
Testing a lamp burns it out — so a factory can only ever test a small sample of its production.
In a random sample every student has exactly the same chance of being picked — all bars equal.

First divide the heterogeneous society into homogeneous layers — then sample each layer by its size.
Set A wages huddle between 170 and 240 — a small dispersion.
Set B wages stretch from 50 all the way to 400 — a big dispersion, yet the same mean!
Same mean of 200 — but look how far set B's bars sit from the mean line.
